description: Practice understanding teacher directions, short school talk, and academic language.

A.range: Classroom support choice; not a WIDA proficiency level
A.studentGoal: I can listen for important words and choose the best answer.
A.objective: I can follow short school directions and explain my choice with a sentence frame.
A.target: Today I will practice listening for actions, main ideas, details, places, and evidence.
A.teacherSummary: Built for grades 6-8 multilingual learners who need clear oral-language routines, visuals, and low-risk responses before ACCESS-style listening tasks.

info.headline: Listen for important words and follow what you hear.
info.summary: Level A builds the foundation of academic listening for newcomer and early-emerging students. Learners practice catching key words in short, slow teacher talk and matching what they hear to pictures, actions, and simple choices. Every task pairs spoken language with strong visual and vocabulary support so meaning is never carried by words alone.
info.distinguishes: Compared with Level B, Level A uses very short scripts (1-3 sentences) read at a slow, clear pace with frequent repetition, heavy picture/icon support, and answer choices that are pictured or one phrase long. Students identify single stated facts rather than connecting ideas or inferring, and sentence frames are provided for every spoken response.
canDo: I can follow a one- or two-step oral direction in class.
I can match a spoken word to the right picture or action.
I can identify spoken numbers, places, and everyday school words.
I can pick out one key detail (who, what, where, when) from short talk.
I can put 3-4 spoken steps in the right order using signal words.
I can complete a short spoken summary by choosing the missing word.

activities.title: Weather Words: Follow a Direction
activities.skill: Follow simple oral directions
activities.directions: Listen to the teacher direction. Choose the action that matches what the direction says to do.
listenFor: where your pencil or eyes should go
vocabulary: draw a round line around something
encerrar en un círculo: dibujar una línea redonda alrededor
subrayar: dibujar una línea debajo de las palabras
put things together that go together
emparejar: juntar cosas que van juntas
frames: I know because I heard the word ___.
activities.prompt: What does the teacher want you to do with the weather word?

options.text: Draw a round line around the weather word.
Write a new sentence about weather.
Erase the weather word and write it again in the box at the top of the page.

activities.correct: Yes. Circle means draw a round line around the word. You matched the action to the direction.
activities.hint: Listen for the action word. What does circle tell your hand to do?
activities.support: Model: If the teacher says circle, I look for the answer with a round line.
activities.extension: Say it in one sentence: The direction says to ___.

teacher.use: Use as a 10-minute warm-up before independent ACCESS practice.
teacher.function: Interpret imperative classroom language.
teacher.lower: Read each option aloud and let students point before clicking.
teacher.onLevel: Ask students to repeat the action word before answering.
teacher.challenge: Have students write one new direction using circle, underline, or match.
teacher.noTech: Print the activity and have students mark the matching action.
teacher.prompt: Which word helped you know what to do?

activities.script: Look at the list of words at the top of your page. Circle the word that names today's weather, like sunny or rainy.

distractorFeedback.b: The teacher does not ask for new writing. Listen again for the one action word that tells your pencil what to do.
distractorFeedback.c: Nothing in the direction tells you to erase or copy. The action word means you mark the word where it already is.

activities.title: What Plants Need: Listen for the Main Idea
activities.skill: Identify the main idea
activities.directions: Listen to a short teacher statement. Choose what it is mostly about.
vocabulary: what the whole message is mostly about
idea principal: de qué trata todo el mensaje
frames: The detail is ___, but the main idea is ___.
activities.prompt: What is the teacher's main idea?

options.text: The bean plant in the closet turned pale.
Plants need things to grow and stay healthy.
The plant is green and it has many leaves on its long stem near the window.

activities.correct: Correct. The whole statement is about what plants need to grow. The other answers are details or extra ideas.
activities.hint: Ask: What is the teacher mostly talking about from beginning to end?
activities.support: Model: Sunlight, water, and space are details. Together they show the main idea: plants need things to grow.
activities.extension: Explain your choice: I chose ___ because the statement is mostly about ___.

teacher.use: Station activity for distinguishing details from main ideas.
teacher.function: Identify and summarize an oral academic message.
teacher.lower: Cover two options first, then compare the best two choices.
teacher.onLevel: Ask students to say one detail and then the main idea.
teacher.challenge: Have students create a new main idea option and one detail-only distractor.
teacher.noTech: Read the prompt twice and let students hold up A, B, or C cards.
teacher.prompt: Why is one answer bigger than the others?

activities.script: In our class garden, we learned that plants need three things to grow: sunlight, water, and space. The bean plant we kept in the dark closet turned pale and weak. The seedlings crowded into one small pot stayed tiny. Without these things, plants may not stay healthy.

distractorFeedback.b: That is one example the teacher gives. The main idea has to cover the closet plant, the crowded pot, and everything else.
distractorFeedback.c: The teacher never describes a green plant by a window. Choose the idea the whole talk keeps coming back to.

activities.prompt: Where will Maya go after lunch?

options.text: to the library
to lunch
to science class

activities.correct: Yes. The place detail is library. Lunch tells when, and science notebook tells what.
activities.hint: The question asks where. Listen for the place word.
activities.support: Model: I ask, where will she go? The place word is library, so I choose library.
activities.extension: Use the frame: The detail I heard was ___.

teacher.use: Small-group detail tracking with oral rereads.
teacher.function: Locate specific information in a short oral text.
teacher.lower: Preview who/where/when before reading the prompt.
teacher.onLevel: Students complete the tracker before answering.
teacher.challenge: Ask students to write a new who/where/when question.
teacher.noTech: Students fold paper into who, where, when boxes.
teacher.prompt: Which answer tells the place, not the time or object?

activities.script: Good afternoon, eighth graders. This is Mr. Dunn with a reminder from the media center. After lunch today, Maya will return her science notebook to the library, because she left it behind during yesterday’s lab. Maya, please bring your library card so the librarian can check the notebook in.

distractorFeedback.b: Lunch tells when Maya goes, not where. Listen for the place where she returns her notebook.
distractorFeedback.c: Science describes her notebook and yesterday’s lab, not where she is going. Listen for the place where the notebook is returned.

activities.title: Solid, Liquid, or Gas?
activities.skill: Sort science details from a short talk
wida: Classify details from a science talk
activities.directions: Listen to the science teacher. Then sort each thing into the state of matter the teacher gives it. Use the buttons; no dragging is needed.
vocabulary: matter that keeps its own shape
sólido: materia que mantiene su propia forma
matter that flows and takes the shape of its container
líquido: materia que fluye y toma la forma de su recipiente
matter that spreads out to fill all the space it is in
gas: materia que se expande para llenar todo el espacio donde está
frames: I heard the teacher say ___, so I chose ___.

items.text: Ice cube
Milk
Air inside a balloon
Wooden block
Steam above hot soup
Melted butter

activities.correct: Yes. Ice and a block keep their shape, milk and melted butter flow, and air and steam spread out to fill space.
activities.hint: Listen for what each state does: keeps its shape, flows, or spreads out to fill space.
activities.support: Model: Milk flows and takes the shape of the cup, so milk is a liquid.
activities.extension: Name one more solid, liquid, and gas from your kitchen. Say: ___ is a ___ because it ___.

teacher.use: Science warm-up before a states-of-matter lesson; play the talk twice.
teacher.function: Classify objects from a spoken science explanation.
teacher.lower: Sort only ice cube, milk, and air first; show real objects if you can.
teacher.onLevel: Students sort all six and explain one choice with because.
teacher.challenge: Students explain why melted butter and steam are tricky.
teacher.noTech: Read the talk aloud; students sort word cards into three columns.
teacher.prompt: Which thing was hardest to sort, and what did the teacher say about it?

activities.prompt: Is each thing a solid, a liquid, or a gas?
activities.script: Today we are learning about three states of matter. A solid keeps its own shape. An ice cube is a solid, and so is a wooden block. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. Milk is a liquid. Melted butter is a liquid, too. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it is in. The air inside a balloon is a gas. The steam above a pot of hot soup is also a gas.

itemFeedback.s1: Ice keeps its shape when you hold it. Listen for what the teacher says keeps its own shape.
itemFeedback.s2: Milk takes the shape of the cup you pour it into. Which state flows?
itemFeedback.s3: Air spreads out to fill the whole balloon. Which state fills all the space it is in?
itemFeedback.s4: A block does not flow or spread out. Does it keep its own shape?
itemFeedback.s5: Steam rises and spreads into the air above the pot. It is not the soup itself.
itemFeedback.s6: The teacher said melted butter. Melted butter flows like milk; it does not keep a shape.

activities.title: Compare Decimals: Listen for the Larger Amount
activities.skill: Understand simple academic directions
activities.directions: Listen to the academic prompt. Choose what the student should do.
vocabulary: tell how two things are alike or different
comparar: decir en qué se parecen o difieren
write the name of a part
etiquetar: escribir el nombre de una parte
más grande: mayor en tamaño o cantidad
diagrama: una imagen que enseña información
activities.prompt: Which choice follows the math direction?

options.text: Choose 0.07 because it has more digits.
Say the two numbers are equal because both have a 7.
Choose 0.7 because seven tenths is larger than seven hundredths.

activities.correct: Correct. Compare means look at both numbers, and larger means choose the greater amount.
activities.hint: Find the academic verbs: compare and choose. Then look for the larger number.
activities.support: Model: 0.7 is seven tenths. 0.07 is seven hundredths. Tenths are larger pieces than hundredths.
activities.extension: Use the frame: The student should ___ because ___.

teacher.use: ACCESS prep connection to math/science classroom directions.
teacher.function: Interpret academic verbs in oral directions.
teacher.lower: Preteach compare, choose, and larger with gestures.
teacher.onLevel: Students explain the chosen number using tenths/hundredths.
teacher.challenge: Students write another compare prompt using fractions or measurements.
teacher.noTech: Read the prompt and let students annotate the academic verbs.
teacher.prompt: Which words tell the student what action to take?

activities.script: Class, compare the two numbers on the board and choose the larger amount: zero point seven, or zero point zero seven. Think about the place value of each seven before you decide. Then write your choice and one reason on your whiteboard.

distractorFeedback.b: More digits does not mean a larger amount. Think about the place value of the 7 in each number you heard.
distractorFeedback.c: Both numbers have a 7, but it sits in a different place. Tenths and hundredths are not the same size.

activities.title: The Lab Sheet: Listen for the Order Word
activities.skill: Combine listening and evidence
activities.directions: Answer the mixed listening question. Then say or write one evidence sentence.
vocabulary: evidencia: palabras que prueban tu respuesta
tell why your answer makes sense
explicar: decir por qué tu respuesta tiene sentido
a word that gives a reason
porque: una palabra que da una razón
activities.prompt: What should students do with a finished lab sheet before they line up?

options.text: Line up at the door and wait quietly until the bell rings for the end of class.
Start a new lab sheet.
Put the lab sheet in the blue basket.

activities.correct: Yes. The word before tells the order: the finished lab sheet goes in the blue basket, and then students line up.
activities.hint: Listen for the order word. What happens before students line up?
activities.support: Model: Before means earlier. The finished lab sheet goes in the blue basket earlier than lining up.
activities.extension: Complete: I chose ___ because the teacher said ___.

teacher.use: Quick exit ticket after the practice sequence.
teacher.function: Use evidence to justify a listening answer.
teacher.lower: Let students orally rehearse the evidence sentence with a partner.
teacher.onLevel: Students complete the frame independently.
teacher.challenge: Students explain why the other answers are not first.
teacher.noTech: Students write the answer and one evidence word on an index card.
teacher.prompt: What word tells the order of the actions?

activities.script: Okay, scientists, we are almost out of time. Please push in your stools and clean your goggles. Put your finished lab sheet in the blue basket before you line up. If you did not finish, write your name on the sheet and put it in the green basket instead. I will check both baskets after school.

distractorFeedback.b: Lining up happens after another step. Listen for the word that tells you what comes before lining up.
distractorFeedback.c: The teacher talks about a finished lab sheet, not a new one. Listen for where the finished sheet goes.

activities.title: Follow the Lab Safety Steps
activities.skill: Following one-step oral directions
activities.directions: Listen to the teacher. Then choose what you should do first.
activities.prompt: What should you do FIRST before the science experiment?

options.text: Pour the liquid into the sink before the teacher says the lab is over.
Wait for the teacher to give the liquid.
Clean up the lab table.
Put on safety goggles.

activities.correct: Great listening! Safety always comes first, so you put on goggles before you touch anything.
activities.hint: Listen again for the safety word. What protects your eyes?
activities.support: The teacher says the word "first" to tell you the order.
activities.extension: What is one more way you stay safe in the science room?
vocabulary: special glasses that protect your eyes
gafas protectoras: lentes especiales que protegen los ojos
a science test to learn something
experimento: una prueba científica para aprender algo
frames: I put on ___ to stay safe.
activities.adminScript: Listen carefully. Before our science experiment today, there are important steps. First, put on your safety goggles to protect your eyes. Then wait for me to give the liquid. Now answer: What should you do first?

teacher.use: Opening routine before any lab or hands-on task.
teacher.function: Following oral directions, sequencing safety steps.
teacher.lower: Read the script twice and point to a goggles picture.
teacher.onLevel: Read once at a normal pace.
teacher.challenge: Ask students to retell all the steps in order.
teacher.noTech: Read the script aloud and have students hold up fingers for first, second, third.
teacher.prompt: Why do you think we put on goggles before anything else?

activities.script: Listen carefully. Before our science experiment today, there are important steps. First, put on your safety goggles to protect your eyes. Then wait for me to give the liquid.

distractorFeedback.b: The teacher never tells you to pour anything. Listen for the safety step that happens before you touch any liquid.
distractorFeedback.c: Waiting for the liquid is a real step, but the teacher says it comes then, not first.
distractorFeedback.d: The teacher does not talk about cleaning up. Listen for the order word and the thing that protects your eyes.

activities.title: Numbers in Math Class
activities.skill: Identifying spoken numbers and quantities
activities.directions: Listen to the teacher. Choose the number you hear.
activities.prompt: How many pencils does the teacher have?

options.text: Twenty pencils
Twelve pencils
Two pencils
Ten pencils

activities.correct: Nice work! You heard the number twenty clearly.
activities.hint: Listen for the ending sound. Twelve and twenty sound close. Twenty ends with "-ty."
activities.support: Numbers that end in "-teen" are smaller. Numbers that end in "-ty" are bigger groups of ten.
activities.extension: Say a number between twenty and thirty out loud.
activities.adminScript: Listen. I am getting ready for math class. I count my pencils. I have twenty pencils on my desk. Now answer: How many pencils does the teacher have?

teacher.use: Warm-up to practice tricky number pairs (-teen vs -ty).
teacher.function: Listening for numbers and quantities.
teacher.lower: Hold up a card with 20 written on it after reading.
teacher.onLevel: Read at normal speed once.
teacher.challenge: Use two-digit numbers and a short word problem.
teacher.noTech: Read aloud and have students write the number on a whiteboard.
teacher.prompt: How is twenty different from twelve when you say them?

activities.script: Listen. I am getting ready for math class. I count my pencils. I have twenty pencils on my desk.

distractorFeedback.a: Twelve sounds close, but it is not the number you heard. Listen to how the number word ends.
distractorFeedback.c: Two is much smaller than the number the teacher says. Listen to the whole number word again.
distractorFeedback.d: Ten is not the number the teacher counts. Listen to the last sentence again for the exact number.

activities.title: Measure a Liquid
activities.skill: Order the steps of a science procedure you hear
activities.directions: Listen to the science teacher. Put the steps for measuring a liquid in order.
vocabulary: a tall tube with lines for measuring liquids
probeta graduada: un tubo alto con líneas para medir líquidos
a small unit for measuring liquids (mL)
mililitro: una unidad pequeña para medir líquidos (mL)
al nivel: a la misma altura
activities.prompt: Put the measuring steps in the order the teacher says to do them.

items.text: Set the cylinder on a flat desk.
Pour the water in slowly.
Bend down so your eyes are level with the water.
Read the number at the bottom of the curve.
Write the amount and the unit.

activities.correct: Yes. Set the cylinder down, pour, get your eyes level, read at the bottom of the curve, then record the amount with its unit.
activities.hint: Listen for first, next, before, and last. Before you read tells you which step comes ahead of reading.
activities.support: Model: You bend down before you read, so bending comes ahead of reading.
activities.extension: Tell a partner why you write the unit, milliliters, with the number.

teacher.use: Science lab-skills listening task before students measure liquids.
teacher.function: Sequence a spoken lab procedure, including a step introduced with before.
teacher.lower: Model each step with a real cylinder while the talk plays.
teacher.onLevel: Students order all five steps and explain where the before step goes.
teacher.challenge: Students explain why reading from above gives a wrong number.
teacher.noTech: Read the steps aloud; students number step strips.
teacher.prompt: Why does the teacher say before you read the number?

activities.script: Today you will measure water with a graduated cylinder. First, set the cylinder on a flat desk so it does not tip. Next, pour the water in slowly. Before you read the number, bend down so your eyes are level with the water. The top of the water curves a little. Read the number at the bottom of the curve. Last, write the amount in your notebook, and add the unit, milliliters.

itemFeedback.i1: The cylinder must be steady before any water goes in. Listen for why it should not tip.
itemFeedback.i2: You cannot read an amount until there is water in the cylinder.
itemFeedback.i3: The teacher said to do this before you read the number. It happens after the water is in.
itemFeedback.i4: You read the number only after your eyes are level with the water.
itemFeedback.i5: You can only write an amount after you have read it.

info.headline: Listen for reasons, main ideas, and academic details in school talk.
info.summary: Level B moves students from catching key words to understanding connected academic discourse. Learners follow multi-step explanations, track several supporting details across a passage, distinguish main idea from detail, and use clues to infer speakers, causes, and effects. Tasks use content-area talk from math, science, social studies, and technology and ask students to explain their thinking with evidence.
info.distinguishes: Compared with Level A, Level B uses longer connected passages (4-8 sentences) read at near-natural pace with less repetition and lighter visual support. Students integrate information across a passage, infer unstated meaning, and justify answers, instead of identifying a single stated fact. Response types expand to multi-select, hot-text, and constructed responses where students produce their own academic language.

activities.title: Listen: Why Leaves Change Color
activities.skill: Identifying the main idea of a science mini-lecture
activities.directions: Listen to a short science lecture. Then choose the sentence that best states its main idea.
activities.prompt: What is the main idea of the lecture?
activities.script: Today we are going to answer a question many of you asked: why do leaves change color in the fall? Leaves look green in summer because they are full of chlorophyll, the pigment plants use to capture sunlight for photosynthesis. But chlorophyll is not the only pigment in a leaf. Yellow and orange pigments are there all summer long; the green simply covers them up. In the fall, days get shorter and cooler, so trees slow down and stop making new chlorophyll. As the green breaks down, the yellow and orange colors finally show. Some trees, like red maples, also make new red pigments in the fall. So the colors we see are not painted on in autumn. Most of them were hiding in the leaf the whole time.

options.text: Red maples are the most colorful trees in the fall because they grow in cold soil near rivers and streams, and they get extra water from the rain.
Trees need more sunlight in the fall than in the summer.
Chlorophyll is the pigment that makes leaves turn orange.
Fall colors appear mainly because green chlorophyll breaks down and reveals pigments that were already there.

activities.correct: Exactly. The whole lecture builds to one idea: the colors were hiding under the green, and they show when chlorophyll breaks down.
activities.hint: The main idea is the point the whole talk supports, often repeated at the end. Listen to the last two sentences.
activities.support: A detail (like red maples) is true but too small. The main idea answers the question the speaker asked at the start.
activities.extension: Explain in one sentence why shorter days cause trees to stop making chlorophyll.

activities.directions: Listen to two students, Amara and Diego, discuss how to spend the student council budget. Then answer the question.
activities.prompt: What do BOTH speakers agree on?
activities.script: Amara: I think the student council should spend this year's money on a bottle-filling water station in the gym. Diego: I agree that the plastic problem is real, and I agree that students need more water during the day. But the gym already has a water fountain. activities.title: Listen: How the Erie Canal Changed a Nation
activities.skill: Identifying several effects in a history mini-lecture
activities.directions: Listen to a social studies mini-lecture about the Erie Canal. Choose ALL the effects the speaker describes.
activities.prompt: Which effects of the Erie Canal does the speaker describe?
activities.script: When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, it connected the Great Lakes to the Hudson River, and from there to New York City and the Atlantic Ocean. Before the canal, moving a ton of grain from Buffalo to New York City by wagon cost about one hundred dollars and took around two weeks. After the canal opened, the same trip cost about ten dollars and took about eight days. Because shipping became so much cheaper, farmers in Ohio and Michigan could suddenly sell their crops in eastern cities. New York City grew into the busiest port in the country. Towns like Rochester and Syracuse sprang up along the canal's banks. Historians often say the canal helped turn New York into the Empire State.

options.text: The cost of shipping goods dropped sharply.
Western farmers could sell crops in eastern markets.
Railroads were no longer needed in New York.
New towns grew up along the canal.

activities.correct: Strong listening. The speaker named cheaper shipping, new markets for western farmers, and new canal towns. Railroads were never mentioned.
activities.hint: Listen for cause-and-effect signals: "because," "after the canal opened," and "sprang up." One choice was never said.
activities.support: An effect is a result. Ask: what changed AFTER 1825? Then check each choice against what you heard.
activities.extension: Which effect do you think mattered most to the country? Explain using one number from the lecture.
wida: Identify multiple effects in academic talk

activities.title: Listen: Which Evidence Is Strongest?
activities.skill: Evaluating the strength of spoken evidence
activities.directions: Listen to a peer discussion about homework. Then decide which piece of evidence best supports Mei's claim.
activities.prompt: Which evidence BEST supports Mei's claim that homework should be limited to one hour a night?
activities.script: Mei: I think middle school homework should be limited to one hour a night. Omar: Why one hour? Mei: Well, a lot of people say homework is stressful. My cousin says she hates it. Omar: That is just one person. Mei: Okay, but our class survey found that students who did more than two hours a night reported sleeping almost an hour less than students who did one hour or less. And the school nurse told us that students our age need nine to twelve hours of sleep. Omar: Hmm. Also, homework might be boring, right? Mei: Maybe, but boring is not really the point. The point is sleep.

options.text: Mei's cousin says she hates homework, and she says it every single day after school with her friends.
Omar thinks homework might be boring.
The class survey linked more homework time to less sleep.
A lot of people say homework is stressful.

activities.correct: Right. The survey is data from many students, and it connects directly to Mei's reason: sleep. The others are opinions or one person's feelings.
activities.hint: Strong evidence is specific, comes from more than one person, and connects to the claim. Weak evidence is one opinion or a vague "people say."
activities.support: Ask three questions about evidence: Is it specific? Is it from a reliable source? Does it connect to the claim?
activities.extension: Explain why Omar said "That is just one person." What is wrong with that kind of evidence?

activities.title: Listen: How Sedimentary Rock Forms
activities.skill: Sequencing a science process from a lecture
activities.directions: Listen to an earth science mini-lecture. Then put the steps in the order the speaker describes.
activities.prompt: Put the steps of sedimentary rock formation in the correct order.
activities.script: Sedimentary rock forms slowly, over thousands or even millions of years, and it happens in a series of steps. It begins with weathering: wind, water, and ice break existing rock into small pieces called sediment. Next, erosion carries that sediment away, often in rivers that flow toward lakes or the ocean. When the water slows down, the sediment settles to the bottom in a process called deposition. Over time, layer after layer piles up, and the weight of the upper layers presses down on the lower ones. This pressing is called compaction. Finally, minerals dissolved in the water act like glue and cement the pieces together. That last step, cementation, turns loose sediment into solid rock.

items.text: Sediment settles to the bottom when the water slows down.
Minerals cement the pieces together into solid rock.
Wind, water, and ice break rock into small pieces.
The weight of upper layers presses the lower layers together.
Rivers carry the sediment away.

activities.correct: Excellent. Weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction, cementation: you followed the whole process.
activities.hint: Listen for sequence signals: "It begins with," "Next," "When," "Over time," and "Finally."
activities.support: Each step has a science name: weathering (break), erosion (carry), deposition (settle), compaction (press), cementation (glue).
activities.extension: Explain why sedimentary rock often has visible layers.

activities.title: Listen: What Went Wrong in the Lab?
activities.skill: Inferring a conclusion from a peer discussion
activities.directions: Listen to a lab group talk about their plant experiment. Then make an inference.
activities.prompt: What can you infer about why the group's results are not reliable?
activities.script: Kenji: Okay, so plant A got the plant food and plant B got only water. Plant A grew nine centimeters and plant B grew four. So plant food works, right? Lucía: Maybe. But remember, plant A was on the windowsill the whole time. Kenji: And plant B? Lucía: It was on the shelf by the door, because the windowsill only had room for one pot. Kenji: Oh. And didn't plant B get watered less over the long weekend? Lucía: Yeah, the custodian only watered the windowsill. Kenji: Hmm. So we can't really say it was the plant food.

The group measured the plants with the wrong tool.

activities.correct: Great inference. Plant A got more light AND more water, not just plant food. With several differences, the group cannot know which one caused the growth.

activities.support: A fair test changes only ONE thing. If light, water, and plant food are all different, the results are not reliable.

activities.script: Let's say a store sells rice two ways. A four-pound bag costs six dollars, and a ten-pound bag costs thirteen dollars. Which is the better buy? For the small bag, six dollars divided by four pounds is one dollar and fifty cents per pound. For the large bag, thirteen dollars divided by ten pounds is one dollar and thirty cents per pound. The large bag has the lower unit rate, so it is the better buy, as long as your family will use all that rice.

activities.title: Listen: Two Views on a Later School Start
activities.skill: Attributing claims to two different speakers
activities.directions: Listen to two speakers at a school board meeting discuss starting school later. Sort each idea by the speaker who said it.
activities.prompt: Who said each idea: Dr. Haddad or Mr. Okafor?
activities.script: Dr. Haddad, a pediatrician: Research shows that teenagers' sleep cycles shift during puberty, so most teens cannot fall asleep before eleven at night. When school starts at seven-thirty, many of them are getting only six or seven hours of sleep. Schools that moved their start time to eight-thirty saw better attendance and fewer car accidents among teen drivers. Mr. Okafor, a parent: I understand the sleep research, but a later start creates real problems for families. Many parents leave for work at seven and cannot wait with their children. A later dismissal would also push after-school sports and jobs into the evening. Before we change the schedule, the district should survey families about transportation.

Many parents leave for work before a later start time.
Schools with later starts saw better attendance.
Sports and jobs would be pushed into the evening.
The district should survey families first.
Teen drivers had fewer car accidents.

activities.title: Listen and Summarize: The Silk Road

activities.directions: Listen to a mini-lecture about the Silk Road. Then write a two- or three-sentence summary with the main idea and two key details.
activities.prompt: Summarize the lecture in your own words. Include the main idea and two important details.
activities.script: The Silk Road was not one road. It was a network of trade routes that stretched more than four thousand miles, linking China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean world. It got its name from Chinese silk, which was so valuable in Rome that only wealthy people could afford it. But silk was only one of many goods. Merchants carried spices, paper, glass, horses, and precious metals in both directions. Even more important than the goods were the ideas that traveled with them. Merchants traded goods such as silk, spices, and glass in both directions, and, even more importantly, religions like Buddhism and inventions like papermaking spread along the same routes.

activities.title: Listen: Why the Wind Blows Off the Ocean
activities.skill: Following a cause-and-effect explanation in science
activities.directions: Listen to a short science talk about winds at the beach. Then choose the best answer to the question.
activities.prompt: According to the speaker, why does the wind blow from the ocean toward the land in the afternoon?
activities.script: Have you ever noticed that on a sunny afternoon, the wind at the beach usually blows from the water toward the land? That is called a sea breeze, and it starts with the sun. Land heats up faster than water does. During the day, the warm land heats the air above it, and warm air rises. As that air lifts away, cooler air from over the ocean slides in to take its place. That moving air is the breeze you feel on your face. At night, the pattern flips. The land cools off quickly, but the water stays warmer, so the air over the water rises and the wind blows out toward the sea. The breeze changes direction because land and water heat up and cool down at different speeds.

activities.correct: Right. Warm air rises over the hot land, and cooler air from the ocean moves in to fill the space. That moving air is the sea breeze.
activities.hint: Listen for what happens to warm air first. Then ask: what has to move in when that air leaves?
activities.support: A cause makes something happen. An effect is the result. Here, one change in the air causes a second change, and the second change is the wind you feel.
activities.extension: Explain in one or two sentences why the wind at the beach changes direction at night.

activities.script: Let's follow a glass of tap water backward to the treatment plant. When river water first arrives, it passes through big metal screens that catch sticks, leaves, and trash. activities.title: Listen and Explain: The Gift of the Nile

activities.script: The ancient Egyptians said that Egypt was the gift of the Nile, and the flood is the reason. Each summer, heavy rain far to the south sent water down the river, and the Nile spilled over its banks. When the water went back down in the fall, it left behind a layer of rich black soil called silt. Farmers planted wheat and barley in that soil and harvested plenty, even though the land beyond the river was desert. Extra grain meant that not everyone had to farm. activities.script: Chair: The student council has nine hundred dollars for the courtyard. We will hear two proposals. Priya: I propose shade sails over the south side. I asked forty students at lunch, and twenty-seven said the courtyard is too hot to sit in by noon. Marcus: I propose four picnic tables. Right now about thirty students sit on the ground. I counted them on two lunch days. Priya: Tables in full sun will still be too hot. Marcus: That may be true. I did not measure the temperature, and my count covers only two days. itemFeedback.s4: The request for approval comes after the plan and its needs have been explained.
itemFeedback.s5: The promise to report comes last, after the trial has been requested.

items.text: The speaker promises to report the results.
The speaker names a problem: broken items are thrown away.
The speaker proposes a solution: a monthly Repair Cafe.
The speaker lists what the program needs: tables, tools, and volunteers.
The speaker asks the committee to approve a trial.

activities.correct: Yes. The proposal moves from the problem to the solution, then the needs, then the request, and ends with a promise to report results.
activities.hint: Listen for the words we propose, we would need, we ask the committee, and after the trial. Each one starts a new part.
activities.support: Read the question first. Play it again and listen for one clue at a time, then check your answer against what you heard.
activities.extension: Tell a partner one more detail you heard and say why it matters to the speaker's message.

teacher.function: Following the structure of a spoken proposal
teacher.lower: Read the script twice, pausing after each idea. Let students jot key words before they answer.
teacher.onLevel: Play once, students answer, then replay and name the clue they heard.
teacher.challenge: Ask students to explain why each wrong choice does not match what the speaker said.
teacher.noTech: Read the script aloud from the teacher page. Students answer on paper.
